test.title: Section 3 · the return of board games

topic.en: A general-interest text: why board games became popular again, in the views of a historian, a designer, a café owner and a sociologist.
topic.kk: Жалпы қызығушылық мәтіні: үстел ойындары неге қайта танымал болды — тарихшы, дизайнер, кафе иесі және әлеуметтанушы пікірі.
topic.ru: Текст общего интереса: почему настольные игры снова стали популярны — мнения историка, дизайнера, владельца кафе и социолога.

paragraphs.text: Twenty years ago, many people in the toy industry assumed that the board game was on its way out. Children were spending more of their free time in front of screens, adults had video games and streaming services, and the tabletop games that remained in the shops were mostly the same few family classics that had been sold for decades. Yet since then, sales of board games have grown steadily in many countries, new titles are published in their thousands every year, and cafés where customers pay to play have opened in cities around the world. Some toy shops that had reduced their shelves of board games have since had to expand them again.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The historian Marta Lindqvist points out that games played on boards are among the oldest forms of entertainment known. Boards scratched into stone or carved from wood have been found at sites thousands of years old, and some games travelled along trade routes, changing their rules as they passed from one culture to another. “People have always wanted a structured way of competing with each other that does not involve physical strength,” she says. “The board game gives them that, and it also gives them a reason to sit together at the same table.”
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: For much of the twentieth century, however, the games sold in shops changed very little. Many of the best-known family games relied heavily on luck, with players rolling dice and moving pieces according to the result, and a single game could last for hours while some players were effectively knocked out early. The designer Tomas Brandt believes that these features gave board games a poor reputation among adults. “A lot of people grew up thinking that board games meant long arguments and boring waiting,” he says. “The games themselves were the problem, not the idea.” Many adults, he adds, had simply never been offered anything better.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The change came largely from a new generation of designs, many of them first developed by small publishers, that reduced the role of luck and gave players more interesting decisions to make. In these games nobody is eliminated before the end, turns are short, and a whole game often takes less than an hour. Some are cooperative, with all the players working together against the game itself rather than against one another. According to Brandt, the best modern designs are “easy to learn but take a long time to master”, which means that a family can play them together while experienced players still find new strategies.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The internet, which many expected to replace board games, in fact helped them to spread. Online forums allowed enthusiasts to discuss and review new titles, and videos showing how to play made it much easier for beginners to learn complicated rules. Crowdfunding websites allowed designers without the support of a large publisher to raise money directly from future players before a game was manufactured, and some of the most successful recent games began in this way. Owen Adeyemi, who runs a board game café, says that many of his customers first heard about a game online before trying it at his tables. Some publishers now test early versions of their games with players online before the final rules are fixed.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Adeyemi’s café keeps a library of more than eight hundred games, and staff are trained to recommend one to suit each group and to explain the rules at the table. Customers pay a fixed charge for the table rather than for each game, and on weekdays groups can stay as long as they like. “Most of our customers are adults in their twenties and thirties,” he says. “For many of them, this is an alternative to going to a bar. They want to spend an evening with friends where they actually talk to each other.” Some groups, he adds, now book the same table every week.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: The sociologist Rosa Ferreira sees this as the main reason for the revival. In her research, people who play board games regularly most often describe the activity as a way of spending time with others without the distractions of phones. “The game gives the evening a shape,” she says. “It gives people something to do with their hands and something to talk about, which is easier for many people than simply sitting and chatting.” She adds, however, that most of her research was carried out with people who already enjoyed games, and that it is less clear how far the trend extends to the general population.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Whether the growth will continue is uncertain. The number of new titles published each year has led some in the industry to warn that the market is becoming overcrowded, and many small publishers struggle to earn money from their games. Rising costs for printing and transport have also made games more expensive to produce, and some publishers have had to raise their prices sharply. Yet the basic attraction seems likely to last. A board game asks people to put aside their devices, sit around the same table and pay attention to one another for an hour or two, and that, for a growing number of people, is exactly the point.
paragraphs.label: H
